question.text: Why is night driving harder than daytime driving?

answer.text: Night driving is harder and more dangerous than daytime driving, because your headlights limit how far ahead you can see.

teaching.text: Driving at night is harder and riskier than by day, because your headlights limit how far ahead you can see. Remember: Headlights limit your view.

audio_scripts.must_match_card_back: Night driving is harder and more dangerous than daytime driving, because your headlights limit how far ahead you can see.

question.text: When should you use your high beams?

answer.text: Use your high beams whenever there are no oncoming vehicles, since they let you see twice as far as low beams.

teaching.text: Turn on your high beams whenever no vehicles are coming toward you, since they let you see twice as far as low beams. Remember: No oncoming cars, high beams.

audio_scripts.must_match_card_back: Use your high beams whenever there are no oncoming vehicles, since they let you see twice as far as low beams.

question.text: How far away should an oncoming vehicle be when you dim your high beams?

answer.text: Lower your high beams while an oncoming vehicle is still at least five hundred feet away.

teaching.text: Dim your high beams while an oncoming vehicle is still at least five hundred feet away. Remember: Dim well before they reach.

audio_scripts.must_match_card_back: Lower your high beams while an oncoming vehicle is still at least five hundred feet away.

question.text: What should you do if an oncoming driver keeps high beams on?

answer.text: If an oncoming vehicle keeps its high beams on, glance toward the right side of the road so you are not distracted or briefly blinded.

teaching.text: If an oncoming driver leaves high beams on, glance toward the right side of the road so the glare does not distract or briefly blind you. Remember: Glance to the right edge.

audio_scripts.must_match_card_back: If an oncoming vehicle keeps its high beams on, glance toward the right side of the road so you are not distracted or briefly blinded.

question.text: When should you switch to low beams while following another vehicle?

answer.text: Use low beams when you are following another vehicle that is less than two hundred feet ahead of you.

teaching.text: Switch to low beams when you are following a vehicle less than two hundred feet ahead. Remember: Following close, go low.

audio_scripts.must_match_card_back: Use low beams when you are following another vehicle that is less than two hundred feet ahead of you.

question.text: Which beams should you use in fog, rain or snow?

answer.text: In fog, rain or snow use low beams, because high beams can cause glare that makes it harder to see; some vehicles also have fog lights for these conditions.

teaching.text: Use low beams in fog, rain or snow, because high beams create glare that makes it harder to see; some vehicles also have fog lights for these conditions. Remember: Fog, rain, snow: low beams.

audio_scripts.must_match_card_back: In fog, rain or snow use low beams, because high beams can cause glare that makes it harder to see; some vehicles also have fog lights for these conditions.

question.text: Where should your eyes be when headlights come toward you?

answer.text: Do not look straight into oncoming headlights; keep your eyes searching the road in front of you.

teaching.text: Never stare into oncoming headlights; keep your eyes moving over the road in front of you. Remember: Eyes on your road.

audio_scripts.must_match_card_back: Do not look straight into oncoming headlights; keep your eyes searching the road in front of you.

question.text: How should you scan the road at night?

answer.text: At night, search well beyond your headlight beams for dark shapes on the road, and glance left and right now and then to find the pavement edge and any hazards from the sides.

teaching.text: At night, look well past your headlight beams for dark shapes, and glance left and right now and then to find the pavement edge and side hazards. Remember: Look past your beams.

audio_scripts.must_match_card_back: At night, search well beyond your headlight beams for dark shapes on the road, and glance left and right now and then to find the pavement edge and any hazards from the sides.

question.text: Should you wear sunglasses at night or on overcast days?

answer.text: Do not wear sunglasses or colored lenses at night or on overcast days, because tinted lenses reduce your vision.

teaching.text: Skip sunglasses and colored lenses at night and on overcast days, since tinted lenses cut your vision. Remember: No tinted lenses after dark.

audio_scripts.must_match_card_back: Do not wear sunglasses or colored lenses at night or on overcast days, because tinted lenses reduce your vision.

question.text: How does added following time differ on familiar and unfamiliar roads at night?

answer.text: Night driving alone calls for at least one added second of following time, while unfamiliar roads at night call for at least two.

teaching.text: At night on familiar roads add at least one second of following time; on unfamiliar roads at night add at least two. Remember: Unfamiliar at night, more time.

audio_scripts.must_match_card_back: Night driving alone calls for at least one added second of following time, while unfamiliar roads at night call for at least two.

question.text: How should you change your following distance at night?

answer.text: At night add at least one extra second to your following distance, and at least two extra seconds on unfamiliar roads at night.

teaching.text: Add at least one second to your following distance at night, and at least two seconds on unfamiliar roads at night. Remember: Add time after dark.

audio_scripts.must_match_card_back: At night add at least one extra second to your following distance, and at least two extra seconds on unfamiliar roads at night.

question.text: What is a work zone?

answer.text: A work zone is an area where roadwork is under way, and it may involve a lane closure, a detour and moving equipment.

teaching.text: A work zone is an area with roadwork under way, which may bring a lane closure, a detour and moving equipment. Remember: Roadwork under way.

audio_scripts.must_match_card_back: A work zone is an area where roadwork is under way, and it may involve a lane closure, a detour and moving equipment.

question.text: How many people does the manual say are injured in work zone collisions each year?

answer.text: The manual says approximately 40,000 people a year are injured in motor vehicle collisions in work zones.

teaching.text: The manual reports that about forty thousand people a year are injured in motor vehicle collisions in work zones. Remember: Tens of thousands hurt yearly.

audio_scripts.must_match_card_back: The manual says approximately 40,000 people a year are injured in motor vehicle collisions in work zones.

question.text: What colors are work zone signs?

answer.text: Approaching a work zone, watch for signs, cones, barrels, large vehicles and workers, and remember that work zone signs have orange backgrounds with black letters or symbols.

teaching.text: Near a work zone, watch for signs, cones, barrels, large vehicles and workers; work zone signs are orange with black letters or symbols. Remember: Orange signs mean roadwork.

audio_scripts.must_match_card_back: Approaching a work zone, watch for signs, cones, barrels, large vehicles and workers, and remember that work zone signs have orange backgrounds with black letters or symbols.

question.text: Should you slow down in a work zone when no workers are present?

answer.text: Always slow down in a work zone even when no workers are present, because narrower lanes and rough pavement can make conditions hazardous.

teaching.text: Slow down in every work zone, even with no workers present, because narrow lanes and rough pavement can still make it hazardous. Remember: Slow even when empty.

audio_scripts.must_match_card_back: Always slow down in a work zone even when no workers are present, because narrower lanes and rough pavement can make conditions hazardous.

question.text: What can happen if you endanger a highway worker?

answer.text: Endangering a highway worker can bring a fine and points on your driving record, under SC Code §fifty-six-five-one thousand five hundred thirty-five.

teaching.text: Under South Carolina law, endangering a highway worker can bring a fine and points on your driving record. Remember: Fine and points.

audio_scripts.must_match_card_back: Endangering a highway worker can bring a fine and points on your driving record, under SC Code §fifty-six-five-one thousand five hundred thirty-five.

question.text: How should you drive through a work zone?

answer.text: In a work zone, slow down, leave a longer following gap, keep track of surrounding traffic and be ready to stop.

teaching.text: In a work zone, slow down, leave a longer following gap, keep track of the traffic around you and be ready to stop. Remember: Slow, gap, watch, ready.

audio_scripts.must_match_card_back: In a work zone, slow down, leave a longer following gap, keep track of surrounding traffic and be ready to stop.

question.text: How careful should you be in a work zone at night?

answer.text: Use extreme caution in a work zone at night, whether or not workers are present.

teaching.text: Drive with extreme caution in a work zone at night, whether or not workers are there. Remember: Extreme caution after dark.

audio_scripts.must_match_card_back: Use extreme caution in a work zone at night, whether or not workers are present.

question.text: How long should you keep obeying work zone signs?

answer.text: Shift your lane position to give workers and construction vehicles room, and keep obeying work zone signs until you see End Road Work.

teaching.text: Shift your lane position to give workers and construction vehicles room, and keep obeying work zone signs until you see End Road Work. Remember: Until End Road Work.

audio_scripts.must_match_card_back: Shift your lane position to give workers and construction vehicles room, and keep obeying work zone signs until you see End Road Work.

question.text: How can you plan for work zone delays?

answer.text: Expect work zone delays and plan for them by leaving earlier, and use alternate routes to avoid work zones when you can.

teaching.text: Expect work zone delays and plan around them by leaving earlier or taking alternate routes when you can. Remember: Leave early or reroute.

audio_scripts.must_match_card_back: Expect work zone delays and plan for them by leaving earlier, and use alternate routes to avoid work zones when you can.

question.text: What should you do on rural roads?

answer.text: On rural roads stay alert, watch for warning signs and obey the speed limit.

teaching.text: On rural roads, stay alert, watch for warning signs and keep to the speed limit. Remember: Alert, signs, speed limit.

audio_scripts.must_match_card_back: On rural roads stay alert, watch for warning signs and obey the speed limit.

question.text: How should you adjust on gravel and dirt roads?

answer.text: Gravel and dirt roads reduce traction, so slow down, leave more following distance and expect that you may skid when you stop.

teaching.text: Gravel and dirt roads give less traction, so slow down, leave more following room and be ready for a skid when you stop. Remember: Less grip, more room.

audio_scripts.must_match_card_back: Gravel and dirt roads reduce traction, so slow down, leave more following distance and expect that you may skid when you stop.

question.text: How should you drive on narrow rural roads without shoulders?

answer.text: Rural roads are often narrower, with ditches or drop-offs instead of shoulders, so slow down, keep centered in your lane and watch for oncoming traffic that may drift into it.

teaching.text: Rural roads are often narrow with ditches or drop-offs instead of shoulders, so slow down, stay centered in your lane and watch for oncoming drivers drifting into it. Remember: Slow and centered.

audio_scripts.must_match_card_back: Rural roads are often narrower, with ditches or drop-offs instead of shoulders, so slow down, keep centered in your lane and watch for oncoming traffic that may drift into it.

question.text: Who generally goes first at a single-lane bridge?

answer.text: At narrow or single-lane bridges drivers take turns, and generally the first driver to reach the bridge has the right-of-way.

teaching.text: Drivers take turns at narrow or single-lane bridges, and the first one to reach the bridge generally has the right-of-way. Remember: First to arrive goes.

audio_scripts.must_match_card_back: At narrow or single-lane bridges drivers take turns, and generally the first driver to reach the bridge has the right-of-way.

question.text: How should you cross open bridge gratings or steel bridges?

answer.text: Open bridge gratings and steel bridges can reduce traction, so slow down, increase your following distance and hold the wheel firmly.

teaching.text: Open bridge gratings and steel bridges can cut traction, so slow down, leave more following room and hold the wheel firmly. Remember: Slow, gap, firm grip.

audio_scripts.must_match_card_back: Open bridge gratings and steel bridges can reduce traction, so slow down, increase your following distance and hold the wheel firmly.

question.text: What should you do at a blind corner on a rural road?

answer.text: Blind corners created by woods, growing crops or steep hills limit how far you can see, so always slow down there and be ready to stop.

teaching.text: Woods, growing crops or steep hills can create blind corners that limit your view, so always slow down there and be ready to stop. Remember: Blind corner, slow down.

audio_scripts.must_match_card_back: Blind corners created by woods, growing crops or steep hills limit how far you can see, so always slow down there and be ready to stop.

question.text: How should you approach a rural intersection with no signs?

answer.text: Some rural intersections have no stop or yield signs, so approach them slowly and be ready to stop for crossing or oncoming traffic.

teaching.text: Some rural intersections have no stop or yield signs, so approach slowly, ready to stop for crossing or oncoming traffic. Remember: No signs, slow approach.

audio_scripts.must_match_card_back: Some rural intersections have no stop or yield signs, so approach them slowly and be ready to stop for crossing or oncoming traffic.

question.text: How should you adjust your driving for snow and ice?

answer.text: South Carolina rarely has extreme winters but sometimes gets snow and ice, which call for slower speeds, acceleration, steering and braking.

teaching.text: South Carolina winters are rarely extreme, but snow and ice do come, and they call for slower speeds, acceleration, steering and braking. Remember: Slow everything down.

audio_scripts.must_match_card_back: South Carolina rarely has extreme winters but sometimes gets snow and ice, which call for slower speeds, acceleration, steering and braking.

question.text: Which road surfaces tend to freeze first?

answer.text: Bridges, overpasses and lightly traveled roads tend to freeze first, and even above freezing, wet conditions can leave ice in shady spots or on exposed roads such as bridges.

teaching.text: Bridges, overpasses and lightly traveled roads tend to freeze first, and even above freezing, wet roads can leave ice in shady spots or on exposed roads such as bridges. Remember: Bridges freeze first.

audio_scripts.must_match_card_back: Bridges, overpasses and lightly traveled roads tend to freeze first, and even above freezing, wet conditions can leave ice in shady spots or on exposed roads such as bridges.

question.text: What is recommended if you must drive in snow or ice?

answer.text: If you must drive in snow or ice, tire chains or special snow tires are recommended, and you should keep the windshield and windows clear and use the defroster.

teaching.text: If you must drive in snow or ice, tire chains or special snow tires are recommended, and keep the windshield and windows clear with the defroster on. Remember: Chains or snow tires.

audio_scripts.must_match_card_back: If you must drive in snow or ice, tire chains or special snow tires are recommended, and you should keep the windshield and windows clear and use the defroster.

question.text: How can you check that your defroster works?

answer.text: Check that the defroster works by turning on the fan and placing your hand on the dashboard.

teaching.text: To check the defroster, turn on the fan and place your hand on the dashboard. Remember: Fan on, hand on dash.

audio_scripts.must_match_card_back: Check that the defroster works by turning on the fan and placing your hand on the dashboard.

question.text: How can a rear-wheel-drive car gain traction in winter?

answer.text: Extra weight loaded in the trunk can help a rear-wheel-drive car get traction.

teaching.text: Extra weight in the trunk can help a rear-wheel-drive car get traction. Remember: Trunk weight helps traction.

audio_scripts.must_match_card_back: Extra weight loaded in the trunk can help a rear-wheel-drive car get traction.

question.text: Why keep a full gas tank in winter?

answer.text: Keep a full tank of gasoline in winter to prevent condensation inside the tank, which may freeze.

teaching.text: Keep the gas tank full in winter to prevent condensation inside it, which may freeze. Remember: Full tank, no condensation.

audio_scripts.must_match_card_back: Keep a full tank of gasoline in winter to prevent condensation inside the tank, which may freeze.

question.text: Should you use cruise control in winter conditions?

answer.text: Avoid using cruise control in winter driving conditions.

teaching.text: Avoid using cruise control when roads are wintry. Remember: No cruise on ice.

audio_scripts.must_match_card_back: Avoid using cruise control in winter driving conditions.

question.text: How should you brake on snow or ice?

answer.text: When you can, drive in the tracks left by earlier vehicles, and brake gently to slow down or stop on snow or ice.

teaching.text: When you can, drive in the tracks of earlier vehicles, and brake gently to slow or stop on snow or ice. Remember: Use the tracks, brake gently.

audio_scripts.must_match_card_back: When you can, drive in the tracks left by earlier vehicles, and brake gently to slow down or stop on snow or ice.

question.text: How much room should you leave on snow or ice?

answer.text: Leave extra room between you and other vehicles on snow or ice, remembering that ice patches may form on bridges even when the roads are clear.

teaching.text: Leave extra room between you and other vehicles on snow or ice, and remember that bridges can hold ice patches even when roads are clear. Remember: Extra room, icy bridges.

audio_scripts.must_match_card_back: Leave extra room between you and other vehicles on snow or ice, remembering that ice patches may form on bridges even when the roads are clear.

question.text: How should you handle hills in winter?

answer.text: Generally avoid hills in winter, and if you must use them, drive slowly at a steady pace with a good gap ahead, since restarting after stopping on a hill may be nearly impossible.

teaching.text: Avoid hills in winter if you can; if not, go slowly at a steady pace with a good gap ahead, because restarting on a hill after stopping may be nearly impossible. Remember: Steady pace, no stopping.

audio_scripts.must_match_card_back: Generally avoid hills in winter, and if you must use them, drive slowly at a steady pace with a good gap ahead, since restarting after stopping on a hill may be nearly impossible.

question.text: What should you do if your vehicle gets stuck in snow?

answer.text: If your vehicle gets stuck in snow, do not spin the wheels; turn them from side to side a few times, use a light touch on the gas and shovel snow away from the wheels and underside.

teaching.text: If you get stuck in snow, do not spin the wheels; turn them side to side a few times, press the gas lightly and shovel snow away from the wheels and underside. Remember: Rock, do not spin.

audio_scripts.must_match_card_back: If your vehicle gets stuck in snow, do not spin the wheels; turn them from side to side a few times, use a light touch on the gas and shovel snow away from the wheels and underside.

question.text: What can you put under the wheels when stuck in snow?

answer.text: To get traction when stuck, pour sand, cat litter, gravel or salt in the wheels' path, or try cardboard, newspaper or brush under the wheels.

teaching.text: For traction when stuck, pour sand, cat litter, gravel or salt in the wheels' path, or put cardboard, newspaper or brush under them. Remember: Sand, litter, cardboard.

audio_scripts.must_match_card_back: To get traction when stuck, pour sand, cat litter, gravel or salt in the wheels' path, or try cardboard, newspaper or brush under the wheels.

question.text: How do you recover from a skid on winter roads?

answer.text: If your vehicle skids on winter roads, lift your foot off the accelerator and steer toward where you want the front of the vehicle to go.

teaching.text: In a winter skid, lift your foot off the accelerator and steer toward where you want the front of the vehicle to go. Remember: Off the gas, steer.

audio_scripts.must_match_card_back: If your vehicle skids on winter roads, lift your foot off the accelerator and steer toward where you want the front of the vehicle to go.

question.text: How does winter braking differ with and without ABS?

answer.text: In a winter skid with ABS, do not pump the brakes but hold steady pressure and expect the pedal to pulse, while with standard brakes you pump them gently.

teaching.text: In a winter skid with anti-lock brakes, hold steady pressure without pumping and expect the pedal to pulse; with standard brakes, pump them gently. Remember: ABS hold, standard pump.

audio_scripts.must_match_card_back: In a winter skid with ABS, do not pump the brakes but hold steady pressure and expect the pedal to pulse, while with standard brakes you pump them gently.

question.text: Should you leave your vehicle in the roadway in winter?

answer.text: If at all possible, do not abandon your vehicle in the roadway.

teaching.text: If at all possible, do not leave your vehicle abandoned in the roadway. Remember: Do not abandon it.

audio_scripts.must_match_card_back: If at all possible, do not abandon your vehicle in the roadway.

question.text: How common is towing a trailer?

answer.text: The manual notes that trailers are towed billions of miles every year, making towing a common everyday activity even if any one person does it only now and then.

teaching.text: The manual notes that trailers are towed billions of miles a year, which makes towing an everyday activity even for occasional towers. Remember: Towing is everyday.

audio_scripts.must_match_card_back: The manual notes that trailers are towed billions of miles every year, making towing a common everyday activity even if any one person does it only now and then.

question.text: What contributes to most vehicle-trailer crashes?

answer.text: Your judgment and common sense are key to safe trailering, and driver error contributes to the large majority of crashes involving vehicle-trailer combinations.

teaching.text: Safe trailering depends on your judgment and common sense, and driver error contributes to the large majority of vehicle-trailer crashes. Remember: Driver error causes most.

audio_scripts.must_match_card_back: Your judgment and common sense are key to safe trailering, and driver error contributes to the large majority of crashes involving vehicle-trailer combinations.

question.text: What are the steps of a correct trailer hookup?

answer.text: Learn the correct hookup for your vehicle and trailer: couple the trailer to the hitch ball, hook up the safety chains and plug in the trailer lights, and finish the whole process without stopping to do something else.

teaching.text: A correct hookup means coupling the trailer to the hitch ball, connecting the safety chains and plugging in the trailer lights, all without stopping to do something else. Remember: Ball, chains, lights, no breaks.

audio_scripts.must_match_card_back: Learn the correct hookup for your vehicle and trailer: couple the trailer to the hitch ball, hook up the safety chains and plug in the trailer lights, and finish the whole process without stopping to do something else.

question.text: What should you check before leaving with a trailer?

answer.text: Before leaving, check that the coupler and hitch ball are properly connected, and make sure both side mirrors are clean and undamaged.

teaching.text: Before you leave, confirm the coupler and hitch ball are properly connected and both side mirrors are clean and undamaged. Remember: Coupler and mirrors.

audio_scripts.must_match_card_back: Before leaving, check that the coupler and hitch ball are properly connected, and make sure both side mirrors are clean and undamaged.

question.text: Why should a trailer be loaded heavier in front?

answer.text: Load a trailer heavier in the front to reduce sway, since failing to do so is a leading cause of vehicle-trailer mishaps.

teaching.text: Load a trailer heavier in front to reduce sway, because failing to do so is a leading cause of vehicle-trailer mishaps. Remember: Front-heavy reduces sway.

audio_scripts.must_match_card_back: Load a trailer heavier in the front to reduce sway, since failing to do so is a leading cause of vehicle-trailer mishaps.

question.text: How should cargo weight be split on a trailer?

answer.text: Put sixty percent of a trailer's cargo weight up front, closest to the towing vehicle, and the remaining forty percent toward the rear.

teaching.text: Put sixty percent of the cargo weight in the front of the trailer, closest to the towing vehicle, and the other forty percent toward the rear. Remember: More weight up front.

audio_scripts.must_match_card_back: Put sixty percent of a trailer's cargo weight up front, closest to the towing vehicle, and the remaining forty percent toward the rear.

question.text: What should you check after a trailer sways?

answer.text: After a sway, check that the cargo is heavier in front and reload if needed, keeping heavy items on the trailer floor rather than stacked on other items.

teaching.text: After a sway, make sure the load is heavier in front and reload if needed, keeping heavy items on the trailer floor rather than stacked. Remember: Recheck the front-heavy load.

audio_scripts.must_match_card_back: After a sway, check that the cargo is heavier in front and reload if needed, keeping heavy items on the trailer floor rather than stacked on other items.

question.text: How should you secure trailer cargo?

answer.text: Pack cargo tightly, secure partial loads with tie-downs or straps and packing material, and never exceed the trailer maker's maximum gross weight.

teaching.text: Pack cargo tightly, secure partial loads with tie-downs or straps and packing material, and never go over the trailer maker's maximum gross weight. Remember: Pack tight, strap down.

audio_scripts.must_match_card_back: Pack cargo tightly, secure partial loads with tie-downs or straps and packing material, and never exceed the trailer maker's maximum gross weight.

question.text: What should you do if your trailer starts to sway?

answer.text: If a trailer starts to sway or whip, steer straight and slow down gradually without braking, never speed up, and stop once you can get completely off the road.

teaching.text: If a trailer sways or whips, steer straight and slow down gradually without braking, never speed up, and stop once you can get fully off the road. Remember: Steer straight, ease off.

audio_scripts.must_match_card_back: If a trailer starts to sway or whip, steer straight and slow down gradually without braking, never speed up, and stop once you can get completely off the road.

question.text: How fast should you drive when towing most trailers?

answer.text: The maximum recommended speed for most vehicle-trailer combinations is fifty-five miles per hour, the posted limit must never be exceeded, and worse conditions call for even lower speeds.

teaching.text: Most vehicle-trailer combinations have a maximum recommended speed of fifty-five miles per hour; never exceed the posted limit, and go even slower in worse conditions. Remember: Slower than normal limits.

audio_scripts.must_match_card_back: The maximum recommended speed for most vehicle-trailer combinations is fifty-five miles per hour, the posted limit must never be exceeded, and worse conditions call for even lower speeds.

question.text: How should you adjust your pace when towing?

answer.text: Towing calls for adjusting your driving to the vehicle, accepting a slower pace, which also saves fuel and lowers the chance of losing control.

teaching.text: Towing means adjusting your driving and accepting a slower pace, which also saves fuel and lowers the chance of losing control. Remember: Slower pace, more control.

audio_scripts.must_match_card_back: Towing calls for adjusting your driving to the vehicle, accepting a slower pace, which also saves fuel and lowers the chance of losing control.

question.text: When should you slow down for a downgrade with a trailer?

answer.text: Slow down before you start down a grade with a trailer, not after.

teaching.text: With a trailer, slow down before you start down a grade, not after you are already on it. Remember: Slow before the grade.

audio_scripts.must_match_card_back: Slow down before you start down a grade with a trailer, not after.

question.text: How much space does a vehicle with a trailer need?

answer.text: A vehicle with a trailer needs more distance to stop and more time and distance to pass, so leave extra space ahead, and even more in rain, snow or fog.

teaching.text: A vehicle with a trailer needs more distance to stop and more time and distance to pass, so leave extra space ahead, even more in rain, snow or fog. Remember: More room to stop, pass.

audio_scripts.must_match_card_back: A vehicle with a trailer needs more distance to stop and more time and distance to pass, so leave extra space ahead, and even more in rain, snow or fog.

question.text: Where should you never pass when towing a trailer?

answer.text: With a trailer, never pass on hills or curves, and remember the trailer does not follow directly behind the car, so turns need extra room.

teaching.text: Never pass on hills or curves while towing, and give turns extra room because the trailer does not follow directly behind the car. Remember: No passing on hills, curves.

audio_scripts.must_match_card_back: With a trailer, never pass on hills or curves, and remember the trailer does not follow directly behind the car, so turns need extra room.

question.text: How do you steer when backing a trailer?

answer.text: When backing a trailer, go slowly with your hand at the bottom of the steering wheel, moving your hand left to send the trailer left and right to send it right.

teaching.text: Back a trailer slowly with your hand at the bottom of the wheel: move your hand left to send the trailer left and right to send it right. Remember: Hand low, move it trailer-way.

audio_scripts.must_match_card_back: When backing a trailer, go slowly with your hand at the bottom of the steering wheel, moving your hand left to send the trailer left and right to send it right.

question.text: What should you do if a trailer starts to jackknife while backing?

answer.text: If the trailer starts to jackknife, stop, pull ahead to straighten out and then start backing again.

teaching.text: If the trailer starts to jackknife while you back up, stop, pull ahead to straighten out and then start backing again. Remember: Stop, pull ahead, retry.

audio_scripts.must_match_card_back: If the trailer starts to jackknife, stop, pull ahead to straighten out and then start backing again.

question.text: Who can help if you are unsure about trailering?

answer.text: If you are unsure how to hook up, load or drive with a trailer, get advice from a trailer professional.

teaching.text: If you are unsure how to hook up, load or drive with a trailer, get advice from a trailer professional. Remember: Ask a trailer pro.

audio_scripts.must_match_card_back: If you are unsure how to hook up, load or drive with a trailer, get advice from a trailer professional.

question.text: When should you walk around and recheck your rig?

answer.text: Before driving and at every fuel stop, walk around the rig and recheck the hitch and coupler tightness, safety chains, lights and tire pressures.

teaching.text: Before driving and at each fuel stop, walk around the rig and recheck the hitch and coupler, safety chains, lights and tire pressures. Remember: Every fuel stop.

audio_scripts.must_match_card_back: Before driving and at every fuel stop, walk around the rig and recheck the hitch and coupler tightness, safety chains, lights and tire pressures.

question.text: What should you do if you hear an unusual noise while towing?

answer.text: If you hear an unusual noise or suspect trouble while towing, stop at a safe place off the road to check it.

teaching.text: If you hear an unusual noise or suspect trouble while towing, pull off the road at a safe place to check it. Remember: Stop off the road, check.

audio_scripts.must_match_card_back: If you hear an unusual noise or suspect trouble while towing, stop at a safe place off the road to check it.

question.text: How should you plan a long trip with a trailer?

answer.text: On long trips, plan rest stops instead of driving straight through, so you drive in daylight while rested and alert.

teaching.text: On long trailer trips, plan rest stops rather than driving straight through, so you drive in daylight while rested and alert. Remember: Plan rest stops.

question.text: What does the safe trailering checklist cover?

answer.text: The safe trailering checklist covers a front-heavy load, a tight hitch, attached chains, working lights, correct tire pressures, reduced speed, thinking ahead, frequent rest, frequent inspection, a secure load and wearing your seat belt.
